briefing.headline: JavaScript runs in two places. This is the other one.
body: You already know JavaScript runs in browsers. Node.js is what makes it run everywhere else — on your laptop, on a server, inside Claude Code. When you ran node scratch.js in M4, that was Node.js. This module explains what that actually means and why it matters.

npm is the package manager that comes with Node. It's how Claude installs the libraries your app depends on — React, the Anthropic SDK, anything else. Understanding package.json and the install/run workflow means you'll stop being surprised when Claude says 'run npm install' and you don't know what that's about to do.

reference.title: npm essentials
reference.content:
npm install              Install all deps from package.json
npm install <pkg>        Install a specific package
npm install -D <pkg>     Install as devDependency
npm uninstall <pkg>      Remove a package
npm run <script>         Run a script from package.json
npm run dev              Most common — starts local dev server
npm run build            Compiles for production

reference.title: dependencies vs devDependencies
reference.content:
dependencies — packages your app needs to run in production. React, the Anthropic SDK, a database client.
devDependencies — packages only needed during development. Bundlers (Vite, Webpack), test runners, linters. Installed with -D. Never shipped to users.

reference.title: What node_modules is
reference.content: The folder where npm install dumps every installed package and all of their dependencies. It can be thousands of files. Never commit it to Git — it's in .gitignore and regenerated from package.json via npm install on any new machine.

reference.title: What package-lock.json is
reference.content: A precise record of every installed package version, including dependencies of dependencies. Commit it. It ensures every machine installs identical versions. If Claude updates a package and something breaks, git diff package-lock.json shows exactly what changed.

reference.title: "Cannot find module 'X'"
reference.content: The package isn't installed. Run npm install <package-name>. Or run npm install without arguments to install everything in package.json.

reference.title: "Missing script: X"
reference.content: The script name in npm run <X> doesn't exist in package.json. Run cat package.json and look at the scripts block to see what's actually there.

completion.headline: M5 complete.
completion.body: You know how Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser, how npm manages packages, and how package.json wires it together. Next up: M6 — JSON.

steps.title: Verify Node and npm
steps.body: You installed Node.js via Homebrew in M0. Verify both are present and check versions — Claude Code and most modern frameworks have minimum version requirements.
steps.verify: Node is v18 or higher. npm is v9 or higher. If either is missing, run brew install node.
steps.trouble: If node isn't found, run brew install node. If it's found but old (<16), run brew upgrade node.

steps.title: What Node.js actually is
steps.body: Node.js is a runtime — it's the engine that executes JavaScript files. Browsers have their own JavaScript engine (V8 in Chrome, SpiderMonkey in Firefox). Node.js took that same engine and made it run standalone, without a browser. That's why you can run node file.js in a terminal. It also gives JavaScript access to things browsers can't do: read files, start servers, connect to databases.
steps.tryCue: Run all three separately. Watch what each produces.
steps.code:
node -e "console.log('Node version:', process.version)"
node -e "console.log('Platform:', process.platform)"
node -e "console.log('Home dir:', require('os').homedir())"

commandNotes.what: Execute a JavaScript expression directly in the terminal without a file. Good for quick checks.
commandNotes.when: Testing a one-liner — converting a value, checking an environment variable, verifying a module is available.

commandNotes.what: A global object Node.js provides — info about the current running process: version, platform, environment variables, working directory.
commandNotes.when: You'll see process.env.VARIABLE_NAME everywhere in Claude-generated server code — that's how it reads API keys stored in .env files.

commandNotes.what: Imports Node's built-in os module. No install needed — it ships with Node.
commandNotes.when: Built-in modules cover common system tasks: os (system info), fs (file system), path (file paths), http (servers). Claude uses them in non-browser code.

steps.verify: You see your Node version, your platform (darwin on Mac), and your home directory path.
whenYoullReachForThis: Claude generates server-side code with require('fs') or require('path') — those are built-in Node modules, no install needed
A Claude Code session reads an API key with process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY — that value comes from your shell environment
Checking what version of Node a project requires vs. what you have installed — compare node --version against the .nvmrc file or engines field in package.json

steps.title: Create a project and init package.json
steps.body: package.json is the manifest for a Node project — it lists what the project is, what packages it depends on, and how to run it. npm init -y generates a default one without asking a dozen questions.
steps.code:
mkdir ~/node-practice && cd ~/node-practice
npm init -y
cat package.json

commandNotes.what: Creates a package.json with defaults — project name from the folder name, version 1.0.0, no description. The -y skips the interactive questionnaire.
commandNotes.when: Starting any new Node project. Claude usually does this for you, but you'll see it in setup instructions.

commandNotes.what: Print the file contents to the terminal.
commandNotes.when: Checking which scripts are available, what version of a package is installed, or confirming Claude updated the right fields.

whenYoullReachForThis: Starting a new app from scratch — npm init -y before any other npm commands
Claude instructs you to create a project directory — this is usually step one
Checking if a folder is a Node project — does it have a package.json?

steps.title: Install a package
steps.body: npm installs packages from the npm registry — a public repository of hundreds of thousands of JavaScript libraries. When you run npm install, npm downloads the package and all its dependencies into node_modules/, and records the version in package.json and package-lock.json.
steps.code:
npm install chalk
ls node_modules | head -20
cat package.json

commandNotes.what: Downloads the chalk package (colorizes terminal output) and its dependencies into node_modules/. Adds it to dependencies in package.json.
commandNotes.when: Any time Claude says "install [package]" — this is what you run. For dev-only tools (linters, bundlers), add -D.

commandNotes.what: Lists the first 20 entries in node_modules. Chalk has its own dependencies, so you'll see more than just chalk.
commandNotes.when: Curiosity or debugging — confirming a package actually installed, or seeing what a package pulled in.

steps.verify: node_modules/chalk exists. package.json now has a dependencies block with chalk and a version number.
whenYoullReachForThis: Claude adds a new import at the top of a file — run npm install <package-name> if the package isn't in your package.json yet
Setting up a project on a new machine — npm install (no arguments) installs everything in package.json
Checking what version of a package you have — look in package.json or node_modules/<package>/package.json

steps.title: Use the installed package
steps.body: Installed packages are imported with require() (older CommonJS style) or import (modern ES modules). Claude defaults to whichever style the project uses. For this practice, chalk uses ES modules.
steps.tryCue: Create this file and run it.
notes: If you see SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement in a module, you need to tell Node this is an ES module. Open package.json in VS Code, add "type": "module" as a top-level field, and run node index.js again.
steps.verify: Terminal shows three lines of colored text — green, yellow, red.
steps.trouble: If you get ERR_REQUIRE_ESM or the import error, add "type": "module" to package.json. This is a common setup step Claude sometimes skips.
whenYoullReachForThis: Claude generates code with import X from 'package' at the top — the package must be installed before this line can run
Switching between CommonJS (require) and ES modules (import) — which one the project uses is set in package.json's type field
A package works in the browser but not Node — some packages are browser-only; Claude should know, but ask if it's not clear

steps.title: npm scripts
steps.body: The scripts block in package.json is where you define shortcuts for common commands. npm run dev starts your local server. npm run build compiles for production. These are how you'll run every project — you don't need to remember the underlying commands, just the npm script names.
steps.tryCue: Open package.json in VS Code and add the scripts block. Then run each.

commandNotes.what: Without a script name, lists all available scripts from package.json.
commandNotes.when: Dropped into an unfamiliar project and need to know how to start it. Faster than reading the README.

commandNotes.key: npm run start vs node index.js
commandNotes.what: npm run start runs whatever command is defined in the start script. Indirection that makes the actual command portable.
commandNotes.when: Always use npm run <script> rather than running the underlying command directly — the script may set environment variables or chain other steps.

steps.verify: npm run start runs the index.js file and shows colored output. npm run lists both scripts.
whenYoullReachForThis: Claude tells you to run npm run dev — that script is defined in package.json and starts whatever dev server the project uses
Setting up a new project with Claude Code — Claude will add scripts; you'll run them
Inheriting a project — npm run tells you what commands exist without reading the whole README

steps.title: Understand node_modules and .gitignore
steps.body: node_modules can contain thousands of files totaling hundreds of megabytes. You never commit it. Any machine can regenerate it exactly from package-lock.json via npm install. This is why the MVE Academy's .gitignore has node_modules/ in it — which you set up in M3.
steps.tryCue: Run these to see the scale.

commandNotes.what: Word count with the -l flag counts lines. Piped here to count how many entries are in node_modules.
commandNotes.when: Counting lines of any output — log files, search results, lists.

commandNotes.what: Disk usage, summarized, human-readable. Shows total size of a folder.
commandNotes.when: Checking how large a directory is before committing, archiving, or deleting it.

steps.verify: You see a directory count and total size. Even a simple chalk install pulls in multiple packages.
whenYoullReachForThis: A Git push is taking forever or GitHub rejects it — you probably accidentally committed node_modules; check .gitignore
Setting up a project on a new machine — delete node_modules if it came with the repo, run npm install fresh
A project's disk footprint is unexpectedly large — du -sh node_modules usually explains it
